Get started with zumir

Source: vignettes/zumir.Rmd
zumir.Rmd

Making R code fast usually means rewriting it in C or C++ and installing a toolchain: Rtools on Windows, the Xcode command-line tools on macOS, gcc elsewhere. Locked-down machines, Shiny servers and slim containers often have none. zumir vendors MIR, a small JIT compiler, so a numeric R function, or a short C function, can be compiled to native code from R with nothing else installed.

library(zumir)

Compile an R function

mir_compile() takes a numeric R function and compiles it to native code. The result has the same arguments and returns exactly what the R function returns. It accepts doubles, loops over indices, conditions and the usual maths; anything else is refused with the construct named. What mir_compile() accepts lists the subset, and every place it errors where R would answer differently.

csum_r <- function(x) {
  y <- numeric(length(x))
  acc <- 0
  for (i in seq_along(x)) {
    acc <- acc + x[i]
    y[i] <- acc
  }
  y
}
csum <- mir_compile(csum_r)

x <- c(1, 2, NA, 4)
csum(x)
#> [1]  1  3 NA NA
identical(csum(x), csum_r(x))
#> [1] TRUE

The compiled loop runs far faster than the R loop, and close to R’s own cumsum(), which is written in C. Timings vary by machine.

x <- rnorm(1e6)
bench::mark(csum_r(x), csum(x), cumsum(x), min_iterations = 10)[, 1:5]
#> # A tibble: 3 × 5
#>   expression      min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc
#>   <bch:expr> <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>
#> 1 csum_r(x)   59.83ms  60.35ms      16.6    7.63MB
#> 2 csum(x)      3.66ms   4.11ms     240.     7.63MB
#> 3 cumsum(x)    4.27ms   4.47ms     225.     7.63MB

So mir_compile() pays off for a loop that R has no built-in for. Examples are a recurrence, where each step needs the one before it, a loop that stops early, and one pass that does what several vectorised calls would do. Where R already has a built-in, such as cumsum(), sum() or vectorised arithmetic, use the built-in. It is already compiled C, and the compiled loop will not beat it. Compile once and call the result many times, because compiling takes time too.

Compile a C function

cfunction() takes the source of one C function and returns an R function that calls it. The source defines one non-static function; static helpers beside it are fine. Arguments named in out are allocated for you and returned, and your own vectors are never changed. Lengths come from the int argument you name.

sq <- cfunction("
  void sq(int n, const double *x, double *y) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) y[i] = x[i] * x[i];
  }", out = "y", n = "n")

sq(x = c(1, 2, 3))
#> [1] 1 4 9

The cumulative sum from above, written in C, comes close to cumsum(). It is a little faster than the compiled R loop, which also does what R does on every step, such as checking for an interrupt.

csum_c <- cfunction("
  void csum_c(int n, const double *x, double *y) {
    double acc = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
      acc += x[i];
      y[i] = acc;
    }
  }", out = "y", n = "n")

x <- rnorm(1e6)
bench::mark(csum(x), csum_c(x = x), cumsum(x), min_iterations = 10)[, 1:5]
#> # A tibble: 3 × 5
#>   expression         min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc
#>   <bch:expr>    <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>
#> 1 csum(x)          1.5ms   4.13ms      251.    7.63MB
#> 2 csum_c(x = x)   1.07ms   3.67ms      292.    7.63MB
#> 3 cumsum(x)       4.17ms   4.35ms      228.    7.63MB

Return a value

A function that returns int or double gives that value back directly.

dot <- cfunction("
  double dot(int n, const double *x, const double *y) {
    double s = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) s += x[i] * y[i];
    return s;
  }", n = "n")

dot(x = c(1, 2, 3), y = c(4, 5, 6))
#> [1] 32

Arguments can be int, double, const int *, const double *, int * and double *. The source may use the C maths library and a few memory and string functions, but it can’t include system headers or call R’s API.

Write MIR directly

mir_function() takes MIR’s textual IR instead of C. It is useful for tests, for learning MIR, and for checking a lowering by hand.

f <- mir_function("
  m: module
     export add
  add: func d, d:a, d:b
     local d:r
     dadd r, a, b
     ret r
     endfunc
     endmodule", "add")

f(1, 2)
#> [1] 3

Native code or the interpreter

zumir checks generated code when it loads. If that check fails, it falls back to MIR’s interpreter: results are the same, only slower. Where MIR has no code generator for the CPU, or the system refuses memory that is both writable and executable, no tier runs and nothing can be compiled. zumir_tier() says which tier this session uses, and zumir_info() says why. You can also ask for the interpreter yourself.

zumir_tier()
#> [1] "native"
zumir_info()
#> $mir_commit
